_meta.method: Compiled from English Wikipedia (Jogye Order, Taego Order, Cheontae, Korean Seon, individual temple articles), official temple sites (jogyeorder.org, musangsa.org, hwagyesa.org, bongwonsa.or.kr, templestay.com), VisitKorea/VisitSeoul official tourism portals, UNESCO Sansa World Heritage listing, and Korean Buddhist Cultural Heritage references.
_meta.coverageEstimate: ~85% of major active Seon practice destinations: all 24 Jogye head temples (bonsa) plus the seven officially designated chongnims, the Taego Order HQ (Bongwonsa) and primary spiritual seat (Seonamsa), the Cheontae HQ (Guinsa), the two main international Zen centers (Mu Sang Sa, Hwagyesa), the Jogye Order's flagship Seon-only training temple (Bongamsa), and several major nun seonwons / Seon practice halls.
knownGaps: Many smaller hermitages (am 암) attached to head temples that host kyolche but lack standalone English presence
Some Taego Order regional bonsa beyond Bongwonsa/Seonamsa
Won Buddhism centers excluded as a separate non-Seon order
Newer urban Seon meditation centers without English-language sources
Several nun-only seonwons (e.g. Unmunsa, Bongnyeongsa) included; comprehensive nun-monastery list may have additional entries
Naewonsa (Yangsan) included from secondary sources; a primary jogyeorder.org listing was not located in English

batch24.scope: 15 high-priority Korean Seon temple records refreshed from popular-only Wikipedia sources
batch24.interpretation: Historical lineage, institutional Seon practice, visitor access, templestay listings, and recurring public practice are recorded separately. Missing public schedule evidence is uncertainty, not evidence that a place is inactive or outside scope.

batch25.scope: 17 remaining high-priority South Korea practice-directory records checked against KTO, municipal, Jogye Order, or official temple/Templestay sources
batch25.interpretation: Historical identity, institutional monastic practice, visitor access, templestay or retreat programming, and recurring public practice are recorded separately. Missing schedule evidence is uncertainty, not evidence of inactivity or misconduct.

places.name: Haein-sa
places.lineage: Korean Seon (Jogye Order — Chongnim, 12th district head temple)
places.notes: Native: 海印寺 / 해인사. Founded 802. 'Haein Chongnim' — comprehensive training monastery. Houses Tripitaka Koreana woodblocks; UNESCO World Heritage (Sansa).

places.name: Songgwang-sa
places.lineage: Korean Seon (Jogye Order — Chongnim, 21st district head temple)
places.notes: Native: 松廣寺 / 송광사. 'Jogye Chongnim'. One of Three Jewel Temples (Sangha jewel). Refounded by Bojo Jinul, 12th c. UNESCO Sansa.

places.name: Tongdo-sa
places.lineage: Korean Seon (Jogye Order — Chongnim, 15th district head temple)
places.notes: Native: 通度寺 / 통도사. 'Yeongchuk Chongnim'. Founded 646 by Jajang. One of Three Jewel Temples (Buddha jewel). UNESCO Sansa.

places.name: Sudeok-sa
places.lineage: Korean Seon (Jogye Order — Chongnim, 7th district head temple)
places.notes: Sudeoksa is a historically important Buddhist temple; VisitKorea gives its heritage, address, open hours, and templestay availability. Its historic association with the Korean Seon training tradition is separate from these visitor facts. A templestay listing does not establish recurring public Seon practice; no recurring public schedule was verified.

places.name: Baekyang-sa
places.lineage: Korean Seon (Jogye Order — Chongnim, 18th district head temple)
places.notes: Native: 白羊寺 / 백양사. Temple and templestay destination; no recurring public Seon practice schedule is established by this visitor listing.

places.name: Donghwa-sa

places.notes: VisitKorea describes Donghwasa’s foundation, address, year-round visitor access, and templestay program. The temple’s Jogye parish and Seon training role are institutional context; no recurring public Seon schedule was verified.

places.notes: VisitKorea documents Hwaeomsa’s history, address, year-round visitor access, and templestay link. Its historic temple identity is not current public Seon practice evidence; no recurring public schedule was verified.

places.notes: The Jogye Order identifies Bongamsa as a special Seon practice center and names Taego Seonwon there. This supports institutional monastic Seon practice; public access and a recurring public schedule are not established.

places.notes: VisitKorea identifies Bongwonsa with the Taego Order, gives visitor information, and describes the annual Yeongsanjae ceremony. These support institutional affiliation, visitor access, and an annual public event, not recurring Seon meditation.

places.name: Seonam-sa
places.lineage: Korean Seon (Taego Order — primary spiritual seat)
places.notes: VisitKorea documents Seonamsa as a UNESCO-listed historic temple and gives its address and visitor access. This supports heritage and visitor context; it does not establish current Seon training or recurring public practice.

places.name: Mu Sang Sa
places.lineage: Kwan Um School of Zen (Korea HQ — Asian head temple)
places.notes: Musangsa’s official site describes it as the Asian head temple of the Kwan Um School, reports year-round group practice including sitting meditation, and says much of the schedule is open through specific programs. This supports current institutional practice and program-based public participation; confirm current dates and access directly.

places.name: Hwagye-sa
places.lineage: Korean Seon (Jogye Order — Seoul International Zen Center)
places.notes: VisitKorea gives Hwagyesa’s history, address, year-round visitor access, and templestay programs. This supports historic and visitor/program context, not a recurring public Seon schedule.

places.name: International Seon Center
places.lineage: Korean Seon (Jogye Order — Seon outreach center)
places.notes: VisitKorea identifies the center as Jogye Order operated and lists Ganwha Seon meditation classes, templestay, Seon culture classes, and a regular Sunday ceremony with a bilingual Dharma talk. This supports current institutional and visitor programming and a recurring public ceremony; it does not establish a recurring public meditation class timetable.

places.name: Lotus Lantern International Meditation Center
places.lineage: Korean Seon (Jogye Order — international branch of Jeondeungsa)
places.notes: The official Templestay directory lists a 2-day/1-night Seon meditation experience and a 3-night/4-day intensive Seon retreat held once a month, with program dates listed through 2026-11-30. This supports recurring retreat programming for participants, not an open weekly public practice schedule.

places.name: Jeondeung-sa
places.lineage: Korean Seon (Jogye Order — historic head temple of Ganghwa)
places.notes: VisitKorea documents Jeondeungsa’s heritage, location, and visitor access. This supports historical and visitor context; no recurring public Seon schedule was verified.

places.name: Naewon-sa
places.lineage: Korean Seon (Jogye Order — major bhikshuni seonwon)
places.notes: VisitKorea identifies Naewonsa in Cheonseongsan National Park, describes its historic Buddha image and temple buildings, and gives visitor information. This does not independently establish its reported bhikshuni training role or public Seon practice schedule.

places.name: Unmun-sa
places.lineage: Korean Seon (Jogye Order — largest bhikshuni gangwon/seonwon)
places.notes: VisitKorea identifies Unmunsa as Korea’s largest Buddhist nunnery and describes a roughly 260-member bhikkhuni community in four-year terms. This supports institutional monastic training context; it does not establish public access or a recurring public Seon schedule.

places.name: Bongnyeong-sa

places.notes: VisitKorea describes Bongnyeongsa’s meditation spaces and lists templestay activities including meditation, prayer, temple food, and tea. This supports institutional facilities and visitor programming; it does not establish recurring public Seon practice.

places.name: Donghak-sa
places.lineage: Korean Seon (Jogye Order — bhikshuni gangwon)
places.notes: VisitKorea describes Donghaksa as an academic institute for female monks and reports about 150 monks studying and practicing Buddhism, alongside year-round visitor access. This supports institutional monastic education and visitor context; it does not establish public recurring Seon sessions.

places.name: Mihwang-sa
places.lineage: Korean Seon (Jogye Order — Templestay flagship)
places.notes: VisitKorea documents Mihwangsa’s history, address, visitor access, and a reservable one-day temple experience. This supports historical and visitor-program context; no recurring public Seon schedule was verified.

places.name: Daewon-sa

places.notes: Native: 白蓮寺 / 백련사. The temple's first-party site is available; venue, lineage, and current public practice schedule remain unverified.

places.notes: Native: 해운정사 / 海雲精舍. Linked to the lineage of Seongcheol; smaller meditation site within Yeongchuk Chongnim sphere.

places.lineage: Korean Seon (Jogye Order — historic Seon-practice temple)
places.notes: Native: 灌燭寺 / 관촉사. Founded 968. Houses giant stone Maitreya.

places.name: Naeso-sa

places.name: Bulyeong-sa

places.notes: Native: 佛影寺 / 불영사. Founded 651. Notable bhikshuni Seon practice site.

places.name: Buseok-sa

places.notes: VisitKorea documents Buseoksa’s heritage, location, and visitor access. This supports historical and visitor context, not a recurring public Seon schedule.

places.name: Daeseung-sa
places.lineage: Korean Seon (Jogye Order — branch of Jikjisa)
places.notes: Native: 大乘寺 / 대승사. Founded 587. Active Seon practice center.

places.name: Hwaun-sa
places.lineage: Korean Seon (Jogye Order — branch of Beopjusa)
places.notes: Native: 화운사 / 華雲寺. Affiliate Seon site under Beopjusa parish.

places.name: Tapsa
places.lineage: Korean Seon (Jogye Order — branch of Geumsansa)
places.notes: Native: 塔寺 / 탑사. Mt. Maisan; small but active practice temple known for stone pagoda complex.

places.name: Heungguk-sa
places.lineage: Korean Seon (Jogye Order — branch of Hwaeomsa)
places.notes: Native: 興國寺 / 흥국사. Founded 1195. Historic Imjin War 'monk-soldier' (uibyeong) base; active templestay and Seon hall.

places.name: Pagye-sa
places.lineage: Korean Seon (Jogye Order — branch of Donghwasa, Mt. Palgongsan)
places.notes: Native: 把溪寺 / 파계사. Founded 804. Active Seon practice hall under Palgong Chongnim.

places.name: Girim-sa

places.notes: Native: 祇林寺 / 기림사. Founded 643. One of the larger temples east of Mt. Tohamsan.

places.name: Borim-sa
places.lineage: Korean Seon (Jogye Order — historic Gaji-san school seat)
places.notes: Native: 寶林寺 / 보림사. Founded 759; Doui's seat — first of the Nine Mountain Seon Schools (Gusan Seonmun: Gajisan school).

places.name: Sudo-sa
places.lineage: Korean Seon (Jogye Order — branch of Jikjisa)
places.notes: Native: 修道寺 / 수도사. Mt. Sudosan. Notable bhikshuni Seon training hall.

places.name: Yeongguk-sa

places.notes: Native: 寧國寺 / 영국사. Founded c. 1052. Historic regional Seon temple; active templestay.
